newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish Islamist-led coalition wins censure battle.
newsitem.headline: Turkish Islamist-led coalition wins censure battle.

text.p: Turkey's Islamist-led government survived a censure motion challenge on Tuesday but was on a collision course with the fiercely secularist armed forces.
MPs voted 281 to 246 to reject two leftist bids to hold a ballot on bringing down Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's coalition for allegedly threatening Turkey's secular system.
"According to this result, the proposals will not be put on the agenda," deputy speaker Hasan Korkmazcan said.
Defeat for the government on Tuesday would have been a major blow to Erbakan and would have opened the way for a full-blown censure motion within a week.
Erbakan, NATO member Turkey's first Islamist leader, is under fire from the country's pro-secular state majority for a series of symbolic measures to increase the profile of Islam in public life.
The powerful armed forces have been among the strongest critics of his coalition with pro-Western conservative Tansu Ciller.
The Milliyet newspaper on Tuesday quoted navy chief Admiral Guven Erkaya as saying he had called on the military top brass to formally warn the prime minister against Islamist militancy.

"A decision must be taken to advise the government so that extreme religious movements do not put the future of the state in danger," Erkaya was quoted as telling a recent meeting of the National Security Council attended by Erbakan.

The prime minister's Islam-based Welfare Party recently urged the lifting of a ban on female government workers wearing Islamic headscarves and called for the construction of mosques in traditionally secularist areas of Istanbul and Ankara.
Tanks paraded on the streets of the central town of Sincan this month after the Welfare mayor allegedly called for governing Turkey along strict Islamic lines.
The tanks' presence was seen as a military warning to Welfare not to encourage staunch Islamism.
The generals have staged three coups since 1960 but they are believed to be cautious about stepping in again unless the Islamists attempt to remove official secularism from the constitution.

"The army would be extremely reluctant to intervene," said a senior Western diplomat. He said the military saw itself as the protecters of democracy and would not want to remove a democratically-elected administration.
